newsitem.title: GERMANY: German states against war pensions to Nazi criminals.
newsitem.headline: German states against war pensions to Nazi criminals.

text.p: Germany's upper house of parliament approved a draft law on Friday to stop disability pensions being paid to Nazi war criminals after U.S. Jewish groups revealed thousands were still receiving such benefits.

The upper house, which represents the 16 federal states, said benefits should be stopped for anyone living in Germany or abroad who had clearly "violated the principles of humanity and justice" during World War Two.
Until now, states could only cut off payments to former war criminals living abroad.
Bonn admitted in January some Nazi war criminals were still receiving pension after a television network said billions of marks (dollars) were being paid out annually.
The American Jewish Committee said that in the United States alone 3,377 pensions were sent each month to veterans of the armies of the Third Reich or their dependents.

"The German government provides generous monthly pensions to Nazi war veterans, whose injuries or even mild, chronic ailments qualify them for 'war victims pensions'," the committee said in an advertisement in the New York Times.

The explosive issue of pension payments to war criminnals surfaced in December, when the World Jewish Congress called on Germany to publish the names of former members of Adolf Hitler's Waffen SS elite forces who live in Britain and the United States and receive disability pensions.
The German government refused, saying strict data protection laws prevented it from releasing such a list.

Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said last month there were still a few such cases in Germany but explained that this was due to a law passed after the war aimed at keeping pension and criminal issues separate.

He stressed that some Waffen SS veterans were still entitled to disability pensions, saying: "The Waffen SS was not just made up of voluntary members, but many were forcibly recruited Germans and foreigners."

The American Jewish Committee also complained that while Holocaust survivors in other parts of the world were eligible to receive German pensions, up to 20,000 Holocaust survivors in eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union had never received any kind of pension from Bonn.

The draft law rules out a general review of all war pensions but said authorities could investigate individual cases when they had concrete evidence that the veteran or widow receiving the benefit had committed crimes against humanity.
The bill now goes to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government, which is supposed to pass it on to the Bundestag, or lower house of parliament, along with its own version of the bill.
If the lower house passes a different version of the bill, it will go to an arbitration committee to produce a common text.
